1	# DataQ — v1 Development Roadmap
2	
3	> **DataQ** — Data quality monitoring platform. The evolution of SnowQ, extended to Snowflake · ADLS Gen2 · S3 · Unity Catalog · ADF.
4	
5	**Stack:** GX Core · FastAPI · React + Vite + Ant Design · Celery + Redis · PostgreSQL · Azure Container Apps  
6	**Timeline:** 8 weeks  
7	**Scope:** Single tenant · DEV / QA / UAT Snowflake environments · Suite-level access sharing

17	| **Datasource types** | Snowflake · Azure Data Lake (ADLS Gen2) · S3 · Unity Catalog (Databricks) · ADF |

56	### ADF webhook receiver (Azure Monitor → DQ platform)
57	- [ ] `POST /api/v1/adf/events` — receive Azure Monitor common alert schema payload, validate shared secret in `Authorization` header, return `200 OK` immediately
58	- [ ] Parse webhook payload — extract `pipelineName`, `factoryName`, `runId`, `firedDateTime` from Azure Monitor alert context
59	- [ ] Follow-up ADF REST API call on webhook receipt — fetch full run details (duration, error message, trigger info) using `runId`

63	> **Security note:** The `/api/v1/adf/events` endpoint must be publicly reachable by Azure Monitor. It is secured via shared secret header validation only — no Azure AD token is issued by Azure Monitor for webhook calls. Do not disable secret validation in any environment.

88	### Severity threshold tiers (warn / fail / critical)
89	> **Design decision required upfront:** agree health score weighting before building — e.g. warn = 0.5 penalty, fail = 1.0, critical = 2.0. This affects the DB schema for run results and cannot be changed cheaply after data is written.
90	- [ ] Add optional `warn_threshold`, `fail_threshold`, `critical_threshold` fields to check model — all nullable; if only one threshold set, check behaves as standard pass/fail
91	- [ ] Alembic migration — add threshold columns to `checks` table and `status` enum (`pass`, `warn`, `fail`, `critical`) to `check_results` table
92	- [ ] Post-processing logic in GX result handler — after GX returns binary result, evaluate observed value against thresholds to derive `warn` / `fail` / `critical` status
93	- [ ] Update check CRUD API to accept and return threshold fields; update run result response schema to include new status values and health score weighting config

140	## Week 5 — Execution engine + scheduling
141	
142	**Milestone:** Async runs with live progress across all datasource types; scheduling operational
143	
144	### Async execution backend
145	- [ ] Celery + Redis background task runner for GX scan execution
146	- [ ] Run progress API — poll endpoint returning per-check live status
147	- [ ] Cancel run endpoint — gracefully terminate in-progress Celery task
148	- [ ] Run history retention policy — configurable purge of results older than N days
149	- [ ] Flat file run path — resolve batch, load via Pandas, execute GX suite
150	- [ ] UC run path — submit job to Databricks SQL Warehouse, execute GX suite
151	
152	### ADF hybrid monitoring (webhook + polling fallback)
153	- [ ] Celery beat task — poll ADF REST API every 10 min for **succeeded** pipeline runs and full run metadata; skip pipelines already updated by webhook within the last 10 min to avoid redundant calls
154	- [ ] Gap recovery logic — on startup and on a 30-min schedule, fetch all ADF run statuses for the past hour and upsert any missed events (catches webhook failures during API restarts or deploys)
155	- [ ] `GET /api/v1/adf/pipelines` — return latest status per pipeline (source: DB, updated by both webhook and polling); used by the UI for display
156	
157	> **Design note:** Webhook handles failure events near-instantly (~1–5 min). Polling handles succeeded runs, run detail enrichment, and recovery from missed webhook calls. The UI always reads from the DB — it never calls ADF directly.
158	
159	### Execution UI

161	- [ ] Live run progress UI — check-by-check status with spinner + cancel button
162	- [ ] Scheduled runs table — create, pause, delete cron schedules
163	- [ ] Recent runs audit table with drill-down link to results

193	
194	**Milestone:** Production-ready v1 deployed to Azure, CI/CD live, team onboarded

196	### DevOps & deployment

203	### Azure Monitor webhook setup (one-time infra, post-deployment)
204	> Requires Azure Container Apps deployment to be live first so the public FastAPI URL is known. Requires `Microsoft.Insights/actionGroups/write` + `Microsoft.Insights/metricAlerts/write` permissions on the subscription.
205	- [ ] Create Action Group (nonprod) — type: Webhook, URL: `https://<nonprod-api>.azurecontainerapps.io/api/v1/adf/events`, shared secret: value from Key Vault
206	- [ ] Create Alert Rule (nonprod) — scope: `lll-adf-nonprod` factory, signal: `Failed pipeline runs`, dimension: all pipelines (tick "include all future values"), action: Action Group above
207	- [ ] Create Action Group (prod) — same config pointing to prod API URL
208	- [ ] Create Alert Rule (prod) — scope: `lll-adf-prod` factory, same signal + dimension config
209	- [ ] Smoke test — trigger a deliberate pipeline failure in DEV, confirm webhook fires, DB updates, and ADF panel reflects failure within 5 min

211	### FastMCP — MCP server
212	> **Library:** `fastmcp` (PrefectHQ). Curated hand-crafted tools mounted into the existing FastAPI app. Each tool calls the internal service layer directly — no logic duplication, but descriptions are written specifically for LLM consumption, not REST API consumers.
213	
214	- [ ] Install FastMCP, scaffold `mcp_server.py`, mount MCP app into FastAPI at `/mcp` — `app.mount("/mcp", mcp.get_asgi_app())`
215	- [ ] Wire Azure AD token validation into FastMCP's auth provider — validate Bearer token on every MCP tool call using the same `verify_azure_ad_token` logic as the REST API
216	- [ ] Implement `list_suites` resource — all suites accessible to current user, name / datasource / env / last run status / check count
217	- [ ] Implement `get_suite_results` resource — latest DQ run results for a suite; pass/fail per check, observed vs expected values, sample failing rows
218	- [ ] Implement `get_health_score` resource — overall health score and 7-day trend, filterable by env and datasource type
219	- [ ] Implement `get_adf_pipeline_status` resource — latest ADF pipeline run status with correlated DQ result per pipeline
220	- [ ] Implement `trigger_suite_run` tool — async GX suite execution against a given datasource + env; returns `run_id` for polling
221	- [ ] Implement `get_run_status` tool — poll live check-by-check progress for a running execution using `run_id`
222	- [ ] Implement `create_check` tool — add a new GX expectation to a suite (form path: check type + column + threshold; or raw SQL)
223	- [ ] Implement `profile_column` tool — run column profiler on a table or file; returns nulls, distinct count, min/max, top values

225	- [ ] Test end-to-end with Claude Desktop — verify tool selection is correct for: "what failed today?", "run the orders suite on DEV", "why did the customer pipeline fail?", "add a null check on email"
226	- [ ] Document MCP connection config for Claude Desktop, Claude.ai, GitHub Copilot (`mcp.json`), and Cursor (`~/.cursor/mcp.json`) in README

228	> **Security note:** The `/mcp` endpoint must be protected with Azure AD token validation. Do not expose it without auth — it provides full read/write access to suites, checks, and execution.

281	| Layer | Technology |
282	|---|---|
283	| Backend framework | FastAPI (Python) |
284	| DQ engine | Great Expectations (GX Core) v1 |
285	| Task queue | Celery + Redis |

312	## MCP tools reference
313	
314	| Tool / Resource | Type | Description | Example natural language query |
315	|---|---|---|---|
316	| `list_suites` | resource | All suites accessible to current user — name, datasource, env, last run status, check count | "What suites do I have in QA?" |
317	| `get_suite_results` | resource | Latest DQ run results for a suite — pass/fail per check, observed vs expected, failing row samples | "What failed in the orders suite today?" |
318	| `get_health_score` | resource | Overall health score and 7-day trend, filterable by env and datasource | "What's the data health score for QA this week?" |
319	| `get_adf_pipeline_status` | resource | Latest ADF pipeline run status with correlated DQ result per pipeline | "Did any ADF pipelines fail overnight?" |
320	| `trigger_suite_run` | tool | Trigger async GX suite execution — returns `run_id` to poll for status | "Run the orders completeness suite on DEV" |
321	| `get_run_status` | tool | Poll live check-by-check progress for a running execution using `run_id` | "Is the orders run finished yet?" |
322	| `create_check` | tool | Add a new GX expectation to a suite — form path (check type + column + threshold) or raw SQL | "Add a null check on email to the customer suite" |
323	| `profile_column` | tool | Run column profiler on a table or file — nulls, distinct count, min/max, top values | "Profile the revenue column in FACT_ORDERS" |
324	
325	> **Auth:** All MCP tools require a valid Azure AD Bearer token. The same token used for the DataQ web UI works for MCP clients. Configure once in your AI tool of choice — Claude Desktop, Copilot, or Cursor — and all 8 tools are available.

> AGENT

Here are the tradeoffs:

**Option A — `backend/` + `frontend/` (flat monorepo)**
- ✅ Simple, conventional, low cognitive overhead — anyone can navigate it day one
- ✅ Single `docker-compose.yml` at root wires everything; no workspace tooling needed
- ✅ Backend (Python/Poetry) and frontend (Node/pnpm) stay fully independent — no cross-language coupling
- ❌ If you later split worker code from API into separate deployables, you end up with `backend/api/` + `backend/worker/` or restructuring
- ❌ No first-class place for shared artifacts (e.g., generated OpenAPI client for the frontend) — usually solved with a `shared/` or `packages/` folder bolted on later

**Option B — `apps/` + `packages/` (pnpm-style)**
- ✅ Clean separation of deployables: `apps/api`, `apps/worker`, `apps/web` map 1:1 to Azure Container Apps / Static Web App
- ✅ Natural home for `packages/openapi-client` (auto-generated TS client consumed by `apps/web`) and `packages/shared-types`
- ✅ Scales better if a second frontend (admin app, embed widget) or second worker appears
- ❌ More upfront ceremony — pnpm workspaces for TS side, but Python side doesn't benefit from it (Poetry doesn't do workspaces well across `apps/`)
- ❌ Mixed-language monorepos in this shape often feel awkward — the pnpm idiom is JS-native, Python sits as a second-class citizen

**My recommendation for DataQ:** Option A. The roadmap has exactly one API, one worker, one frontend — no shared packages today. Option B's value shows up only when you have ≥2 of something. Start flat; promote to `apps/`+`packages/` if a real shared package emerges (e.g., when you auto-generate the OpenAPI client in Week 4–5).

I'll proceed with Option A baked into the plan unless you say otherwise. Drafting the restructured 8-week execution plan now.

Day 3: Flat file + UC execution paths (Snowflake already works from Week 1 probe).\n3. Day 4: ADF Celery-beat poller (10 min interval) + gap recovery (30 min). Day 5: Scheduling UI + run history UI + retention purge policy.\n\n**Risk:** Celery + FastAPI signal handling on graceful shutdown in Container Apps is fragile. Test cancel under load before Week 6.\n\n---\n\n### Week 6 — Results dashboard + alerting\n\n**Exit gate:** A user with no API access can see health scores, drill into failures, and receive Teams alerts when checks fail.\n\n**Sequencing:**\n- Dashboard charts + filter bar first (read-only, low risk).\n- Failed-check drill-down (sample failing rows from GX result) is the highest-value feature — prioritise it.\n- Alerting last, because dedup + suppression + snooze are stateful and need the results pipeline working to test against.\n\n**Design note:** Severity-aware alert routing (warn = quiet, fail = standard, critical = @channel) is only viable if the Week 3 severity tier model is fully wired. Azure Monitor smoke test passes (deliberate ADF failure → webhook fires → DB updates → UI reflects within 5 min).\n\n**Sequencing — strict order:**\n1. Day 1–2: Containerise, push to ACR, deploy to Container Apps + Static Web App. CI/CD on `main`. App Insights wired.\n2. Day 3: Azure Monitor Action Groups + Alert Rules for nonprod and prod ADF factories (`lll-adf-nonprod`, `lll-adf-prod`). Smoke test end-to-end. **Cannot start until step 1 is live** — needs the public API URL.\n3. Day 4: FastMCP scaffold + mount at `/mcp` + Azure AD auth wired to MCP. Implement 4 read-only resources (`list_suites`, `get_suite_results`, `get_health_score`, `get_adf_pipeline_status`).\n4. Day 5: Implement 4 write/exec tools (`trigger_suite_run`, `get_run_status`, `create_check`, `profile_column`). LLM-optimised docstrings. Test against Claude Desktop with the 4 canonical natural-language queries from the roadmap.\n\n**Risk concentration:** This is the highest-risk week. Deployment + Azure infra setup + brand-new MCP integration all converge. Budget at least one day of slack; consider pulling MCP work forward into Week 6 evenings if Week 6 alerting wraps early.\n\n---\n\n### Week 8 — Test coverage gate\n\n**Exit gate:** PRs blocked below 80% coverage. Dry-run works across all 3 source types.\n- **End W4:** UI feature-complete for connection + suite + check authoring. ADF polling fills gaps.\n- **End W6:** Teams alert fires on a deliberate check failure with correct severity routing.\n- **End W7:** Production deploy live. Azure Monitor smoke test green. Claude Desktop drives a suite run via MCP.\n- **End W8:** Coverage gate ≥80%, CI enforcing.\n\n---\n\n## Verification\n\nThis plan is a planning document — verification means stakeholder review, not code execution. > AGENT

Good question — it's a real trade-off. Short version:

**DQX advantages (for the Databricks path specifically)**
- Native to Databricks runtime — no GX-on-Spark shim, no external SparkSession management
- First-class **Delta Live Tables / streaming** support; GX is batch-only
- Built-in profiler optimised for Spark
- Lower runtime overhead (no GX `DataContext` lifecycle)
- Unity Catalog-aware out of the box; respects volumes, governance, lineage

**GX advantages (for DataQ as a whole)**
- **One framework across all 5 datasource types** → one result schema, one suite concept, one serialiser feeding Postgres, one check editor UI model
- Roadmap is *already* built around GX semantics (suites, expectations, checkpoints, result format) — the DB schema, MCP tool descriptors, and severity-tier post-processing all assume it
- The "form-based check editor" in Week 4 is one component; with DQX you'd need a second editor variant for the UC path

**The real cost of mixing them**
Two frameworks → two result shapes → either an abstraction layer (extra week of work) or visibly different result UX between Snowflake and Databricks suites. The roadmap's v1.1 line already calls this out: *"Databricks Live Tables (DLT) expectations — separate execution model from the current GX + Spark path."*

**Recommendation for v1**
Stay on GX for unification. Add DQX in v1.1 specifically for the DLT/streaming use case — that's where GX genuinely can't compete. For batch UC tables via SQL Warehouse (what Week 3/5 actually need), GX is fine.

**If you want me to bake this into the plan**, I'd:
1. Add a "Framework choice" row to the design-decisions table noting GX-only for v1
2. Add a v1.1 callout flagging DQX evaluation as the streaming/DLT path
3. Note in Week 3 that the UC path should keep the GX adapter thin enough to swap later

Want me to update the plan with that, or were you leaning toward DQX-now for UC?

Build the abstraction now; do not hardcode ADF logic and refactor later.\n\n**Design decisions to lock early in the week:**\n- `OrchestrationProvider` interface: `parse_event(payload) -> RunUpdate`, `fetch_run_detail(provider_run_id) -> RunDetail`, `list_recent_runs(since) -> [RunUpdate]`. Both ADF and Airflow implementations must conform.\n- Authentication strategy per provider: shared secret (ADF, matches Azure Monitor's only auth mode) vs HMAC signature (Airflow, since DAG callbacks can compute signatures). Both secrets in Key Vault.\n- `trigger_bindings` schema: composite key (`provider`, `pipeline_or_dag_id`, `env`) → `suite_id`; one pipeline/DAG can map to multiple suites; debounce/dedup behaviour when an event fires twice in quick succession (default: ignore the second trigger if the prior run is still queued/in-progress).\n- Failure-event behaviour: failure alerts the user but does **not** trigger a suite run (no point running checks on data that wasn't loaded). Only successful completions trigger runs. Applies to both providers identically."
}

  "plan": "# DataQ v1 — Project Execution Plan\n\n## Context\n\nDataQ is the v1 evolution of SnowQ — a single-tenant data quality monitoring platform extending GX-based DQ checks across **4 datasources** (Snowflake DEV/QA/UAT, ADLS Gen2, S3, Unity Catalog/Databricks) plus **2 orchestration integrations** (ADF and Apache Airflow — used only for pipeline/DAG monitoring and run-triggered execution, never as DQ datasources). The plan is anchored on the [DataQ_platform_roadmap.md](../../Coding/Python/DataQ/context/DataQ_platform_roadmap.md) — an 8-week, 100-task scope.\n\nThe roadmap is feature-organised (week-by-week, datasource-by-datasource). UI work in Week 4/6 assumes a stable API contract from Weeks 2/3/5.\n4. **Design decisions that affect DB schema land before code.** Severity tiers (Week 3) and the ADF hybrid model (Week 2) both have schema implications — agree weights, status enum, and webhook contract on day one of their week.\n5. **Defer the entire MCP layer to Week 7.** It depends on a stable service layer; building it earlier means rewriting tool docstrings as APIs shift.\n6. **Tests are written in the slice they belong to**, not deferred wholesale to Week 8. Week 8 is the *coverage gate and gap-fill* week, not \"all testing happens here.\"\n\n---\n\n## Critical path & dependency graph\n\n```\nWeek 1: Auth + GX + FastAPI skeleton + DB model\n   │\n   ├──► Week 2: Datasource CRUD (4 in parallel) + Orchestration (ADF + Airflow)\n   │       │\n   │       ├──► OrchestrationProvider abstraction ──────────┐\n   │       │   ├─ ADF: webhook + trigger bindings           │\n   │       │   └─ Airflow: callback webhook + bindings      │\n   │       │                                                │\n   │       └──► Snowflake / ADLS / S3 / UC connection test  │\n   │                │                                       │\n   │                ▼                                       │\n   │       Week 3: Suite + Check API + Profiler             │\n   │                │     (severity tier schema locked)     │\n   │                ▼                                       │\n   │       Week 4: Connection UI + Check editor UI          │\n   │                │                                       │\n   │                ▼                                       │\n   │       Week 5: Celery execution + Scheduling ◄──────────┤\n   │                │              (ADF polling joins here) │\n   │                ▼                                       │\n   │       Week 6: Results dashboard + Alerting             │\n   │                                                        │\n   ▼                                                        │\nWeek 7: Deployment + Azure Monitor alert setup ◄────────────┘\n         + MCP server (8 tools)\n   │\n   ▼\nWeek 8: Unit test coverage gate (80%)\n```\n\n**Hardest dependency:** Azure Monitor alert rule setup (Week 7) requires the deployed public API URL, which requires Container Apps deployment, which requires CI/CD, which requires a green test suite. If Week 8 slips, ADF webhook end-to-end smoke test slips with it.\n\n---\n\n## Week-by-week execution plan\n\n### Week 1 — Foundation (must end with a vertical slice)\n\n**Exit gate:** A logged-in user (Azure AD) can hit a FastAPI endpoint that triggers GX against a Snowflake DEV table and persists a run result row in Postgres. Swagger live at `/docs`.\n\n**Order of operations within the week:**\n1. Day 1–2: Monorepo scaffold + Docker Compose (Postgres, Redis, FastAPI, React, Celery worker all reachable from a single `docker-compose up`). Alembic baseline migration with the core data model (`connections`, `suites`, `checks`, `runs`, `results`, `shares`). **Schema review checkpoint before merging** — see \"Design decisions to lock\" below.\n2. Trigger-binding schema is in place even if the trigger execution path lands in Week 5.\n\n**Two distinct workstreams this week — do not conflate them in the data model:**\n\n**Workstream A — Datasource connections (4 types):** Snowflake, ADLS Gen2, S3, Unity Catalog. Alternative for users who can't add callbacks: Airflow REST API `dagRuns` poller. | Airflow REST API every 10 min (Week 5) |\n\n**Airflow-specific decisions:**\n- **Connection record:** Airflow webserver base URL + auth (Basic / token / Kerberos — pick one for v1, default to token). Build the abstraction now; do not hardcode ADF logic and refactor later.\n\n**Design decisions to lock early in the week:**\n- `OrchestrationProvider` interface: `parse_event(payload) -> RunUpdate`, `fetch_run_detail(provider_run_id) -> RunDetail`, `list_recent_runs(since) -> [RunUpdate]`. Both ADF and Airflow implementations must conform.\n- Authentication strategy per provider: shared secret (ADF, matches Azure Monitor's only auth mode) vs HMAC signature (Airflow, since DAG callbacks can compute signatures). Both secrets in Key Vault.\n- `trigger_bindings` schema: composite key (`provider`, `pipeline_or_dag_id`, `env`) → `suite_id`; one pipeline/DAG can map to multiple suites; debounce/dedup behaviour when an event fires twice in quick succession (default: ignore the second trigger if the prior run is still queued/in-progress).\n- Failure-event behaviour: failure alerts the user but does **not** trigger a suite run (no point running checks on data that wasn't loaded). Only successful completions trigger runs. Applies to both providers identically.\n\n---\n\n### Week 3 — Suite, check, and profiler API\n\n**Exit gate:** Suites with checks can be created, dry-run, and exported/imported via API across Snowflake, flat files, and UC. Profiler endpoint returns stats for all three.\n\n**Critical design decision — must land Day 1:**\n- **Severity tier health-score weights.** Roadmap calls this out explicitly. Agree (e.g., warn=0.5, fail=1.0, critical=2.0) with stakeholders *before* the Alembic migration adds `warn_threshold` / `fail_threshold` / `critical_threshold` columns and the `status` enum. Changing the weight model after results data is written is expensive.\n\n**Sequencing:**\n1. Day 1: Severity tier schema migration + status enum decision committed.\n2. Day 2–3: Suite/check CRUD + sharing + export/import + dry-run (Snowflake first).\n3. Day 4: Profiler service — Snowflake, then ADLS/S3 (Pandas), then UC (Databricks SQL Warehouse). Share a single profiler interface across adapters.\n4. Day 5: Flat file batching regex resolution + UC `spark.read.table()` path + cross-source integration tests.\n\n**Framework note (UC path):** Use GX for v1, but keep the UC adapter thin — wrap the GX call behind an `UnityCatalogCheckRunner` interface so the v1.1 DQX adapter (for DLT / streaming) can be swapped in without touching the suite/check/result layer.\n\n---\n\n### Week 4 — Frontend feature parity with API\n\n**Exit gate:** A user can configure any connection type and author a check end-to-end in the browser. Monaco editor + column profiler panel + dry-run preview + version history drawer is a lot of surface area.\n- Suite sharing + admin pages are the lightest — drop to end of week.\n\n**Recommended technical move:** Auto-generate the TypeScript API client from FastAPI's OpenAPI spec (`openapi-typescript-codegen` or similar). Day 4–5: GX Core wired to Snowflake DEV. One end-to-end probe endpoint: `POST /api/v1/_probe/snowflake-suite` → runs a hardcoded one-check suite → writes a row to `results`. This is throwaway code; its only job is to prove the wiring.\n\n**Workflow expectations for the week (and every week after):** each numbered item above is a separate PR, manually tested before the next one starts. If any item surfaces a defect (e.g., MSAL token validation fails on edge case), raise a GitHub issue immediately; do not patch silently inside the next PR.\n\n**Risks:**\n- MSAL + FastAPI integration is finicky; budget a half-day for token audience/issuer mismatches.\n- GX Core v1's Snowflake datasource API changed across point releases — pin GX version on day one.\n\n---\n\n### Week 2 — Datasource connections + Orchestration integrations (ADF + Airflow)\n\n**Exit gate:** All 4 datasource connection types are CRUD-able and testable via API. Both orchestration providers (ADF and Airflow) accept synthetic event payloads through a unified `/api/v1/orchestration/events/{provider}` route and persist to `pipeline_runs`. Trigger-binding schema is in place even if the trigger execution path lands in Week 5.\n\n**Two distinct workstreams this week — do not conflate them in the data model:**\n\n**Workstream A — Datasource connections (4 types):** Snowflake, ADLS Gen2, S3, Unity Catalog. These live in the `connections` table and feed `suites` → `checks` → `runs`. Independent of each other — split across engineers.\n\n**Workstream B — Orchestration integrations (ADF + Airflow):** Orchestrators are *not* datasources. Both providers implement the same `OrchestrationProvider` interface and do three things and nothing else:\n1. **Monitor** pipeline/DAG runs (status, duration, failure reason) — stored in `pipeline_runs`, not `results`. The table has a `provider` column (`adf` | `airflow`) and a `provider_run_id`.\n2. **Detect failure** in near-real-time via provider-specific event channels (see below).\n3. **Trigger suite execution** on successful pipeline/DAG completion — success event maps to a configured suite via `trigger_bindings` (`provider`, `pipeline_or_dag_id`, `suite_id`, `env`) and enqueues a Celery run. This is the only automated trigger mechanism for v1 (REST API trigger is deferred to v1.1).\n\nNeither provider appears in the suite/check editor as a \"datasource you can write checks against.\" Both appear only in: (a) the orchestration status panel on the dashboard, and (b) the trigger-binding UI.\n\n**Provider-specific event channels:**\n\n| Provider | Failure / success channel | Polling fallback |\n|---|---|---|\n| ADF | Azure Monitor alert rule → webhook `POST /api/v1/orchestration/events/adf` (shared-secret header) | ADF REST API every 10 min (Week 5) |\n| Airflow | `on_success_callback` / `on_failure_callback` in DAG → webhook `POST /api/v1/orchestration/events/airflow` (HMAC-signed payload, signing key in Key Vault). Alternative for users who can't add callbacks: Airflow REST API `dagRuns` poller. | Airflow REST API every 10 min (Week 5) |\n\n**Airflow-specific decisions:**\n- **Connection record:** Airflow webserver base URL + auth (Basic / token / Kerberos — pick one for v1, default to token). Stored in `connections` with `type=airflow_orchestrator`.\n- **Callback adoption is voluntary on the user's side** — we cannot mutate their DAGs. The trigger-binding UI must clearly indicate \"this trigger requires the DAG to POST to DataQ on success; copy this callback snippet.\" Provide a `dataq_airflow_callback` helper snippet (small Python function) in the docs.\n- **Polling is the default fallback** for teams who can't add callbacks; documented as higher-latency (up to 10 min delay) vs callback-based near-real-time.\n\n**Critical path:** Unified orchestration event endpoint + provider abstraction + trigger binding schema must land this week — the trigger execution path and polling in Week 5 depend on it. Build the abstraction now; do not hardcode ADF logic and refactor later.\n\n**Design decisions to lock early in the week:**\n- `OrchestrationProvider` interface: `parse_event(payload) -> RunUpdate`, `fetch_run_detail(provider_run_id) -> RunDetail`, `list_recent_runs(since) -> [RunUpdate]`. Both ADF and Airflow implementations must conform.\n- Authentication strategy per provider: shared secret (ADF, matches Azure Monitor's only auth mode) vs HMAC signature (Airflow, since DAG callbacks can compute signatures). Both secrets in Key Vault.\n- `trigger_bindings` schema: composite key (`provider`, `pipeline_or_dag_id`, `env`) → `suite_id`; one pipeline/DAG can map to multiple suites; debounce/dedup behaviour when an event fires twice in quick succession (default: ignore the second trigger if the prior run is still queued/in-progress).\n- Failure-event behaviour: failure alerts the user but does **not** trigger a suite run (no point running checks on data that wasn't loaded). > AGENT

Yes, several gaps. Grouped by category, here's what's missing — high-value items only:

**Git & branching**
1. **Branching model** — recommend trunk-based with short-lived feature branches: `feature/<ticket-or-short-desc>`, `fix/<issue-N-short-desc>`, `chore/...`. Branch off `main`, PR back into `main`. No long-lived `develop` branch.
2. **Branch protection on `main`** — require PR, require passing CI, require ≥1 review, no force-push, no direct commits, dismiss stale reviews on new push.
3. **Squash-merge only** — keeps `main` history linear and matches working-agreement #1 (one functionality per commit on `main`).
4. **Conventional commits** (`feat:`, `fix:`, `chore:`, `docs:`, `test:`) — enables auto-changelog later and makes PR titles self-documenting.
5. **PR template** with checklist: tested manually? linked issue? security implications? schema migration?
6. **CODEOWNERS** file — auto-request reviews from the right person per area (backend, frontend, infra, MCP).

**CI/CD & quality gates**
7. **Required CI checks before merge:** lint (Ruff), format (Black `--check`), type check (mypy or pyright), unit tests (from Week 8), frontend lint/format/test.
8. **Secret scanning** in pre-commit (`gitleaks` or `detect-secrets`) — and in CI as a second line of defence.
9. **SAST** — Bandit for Python, CodeQL via GitHub Actions. Catches the security-review items between manual reviews.
10. **Dependency vulnerability scanning** — Dependabot alerts + auto-PRs for security updates. Pin Python deps in `environment.yml` with version ranges, lock with `conda-lock`.

**Observability & error handling**
11. **Structured logging from day one** — JSON logs with `request_id` correlation ID propagated through FastAPI → Celery → GX. Pick a logger (recommend `structlog`) in Week 1, not retrofitted later.
12. **PII redaction in logs** — Snowflake row samples in failed-check drill-down can contain sensitive data; redact at the logger level, not at the call site.
13. **Sentry (or App Insights exception tracking)** wired in Week 1, not Week 7. Catches early-week regressions you'd otherwise miss in local dev.

**Database & migrations**
14. **Backward-compatible migrations only** — no `DROP COLUMN` + code change in the same PR. Two-step: deploy code that tolerates both shapes → migrate → deploy code that assumes new shape. Matters from Week 5 onward once real result data exists.
15. **Migration review checklist** — every Alembic PR must include rollback plan and "tested up + down locally" tick.

**Documentation & decision history**
16. **ADRs (Architecture Decision Records)** — one short markdown file per significant decision (`docs/adr/0001-gx-only-for-v1.md`, `0002-adf-airflow-orchestration-abstraction.md`, `0003-severity-tier-weights.md`). Captures *why* for future readers; complements the conversation-driven memory.
17. **`docs/architecture.svg`** — move the existing system architecture SVG into the repo so it lives next to the code.
18. **Local setup script** (`scripts/setup.sh`) — one command from fresh clone to working dev env (conda env + pre-commit install + docker-compose up + alembic upgrade head + seed data).

**Process**
19. **Definition of Done** per task — code merged + manually tested + (from Week 8) unit tests + docs updated if user-facing + issue closed if any.
20. **Weekly security-review checklist** — make the "periodic security review" from your rules concrete: dependency vuln scan results, secret scan results, OWASP top-10 spot check on new endpoints, Key Vault access audit.

---

That's 20 items. My recommendation: **adopt all of them** — none are speculative, all are standard for a multi-engineer Azure-deployed platform handling credentials and PII-adjacent data. Cost is mostly Week 1 setup time.

## Approved Plan (edited by user):
# DataQ v1 — Project Execution Plan

## Context

DataQ is the v1 evolution of SnowQ — a single-tenant data quality monitoring platform extending GX-based DQ checks across **4 datasources** (Snowflake DEV/QA/UAT, ADLS Gen2, S3, Unity Catalog/Databricks) plus **2 orchestration integrations** (ADF and Apache Airflow — used only for pipeline/DAG monitoring and run-triggered execution, never as DQ datasources). The plan is anchored on the [DataQ_platform_roadmap.md](../../Coding/Python/DataQ/context/DataQ_platform_roadmap.md) — an 8-week, 100-task scope.

The roadmap is feature-organised (week-by-week, datasource-by-datasource). This document restructures it into an **execution-oriented** plan: critical path, dependencies, design decisions that must land early, integration seams, milestone gates, and risks. It does not duplicate task lists — it lays out the order, sequencing constraints, and gates that the roadmap's checkboxes feed into.

The repo today is empty (LICENSE + context folder only). All scaffolding work is greenfield.

**Repo layout decision:** flat monorepo (`backend/` + `frontend/`) with a root `docker-compose.yml`. Promote to `apps/` + `packages/` only if a shared package (e.g., auto-generated OpenAPI client) emerges in Week 4–5.

---

## Working agreements (pre-coding ground rules)

These apply across every week and override any conflicting "speed > quality" temptation. If a week's exit gate conflicts with them, the rules win.

### A. Commit & change discipline
1. **One functionality per commit, where possible.** Reviewable units only.
2. **Manually test each committed change before starting the next functionality** — required until the unit test suite lands in Week 8.
3. **Defects → GitHub issue, never silent fixes.** Raise via `gh issue create`. The PR that fixes it must include `Fixes #N`.
4. **From Week 8 onward, every new functionality ships with tests.**
5. **Definition of Done** per task: code merged + manually tested + (from Week 8) unit tests + docs/ADR updated if user-facing or architectural + issue closed if any.

### B. Git workflow
6. **Branching model:** trunk-based with short-lived feature branches. Branch off `main`, PR back into `main`. No long-lived `develop`.
7. **Branch naming:** `feature/<short-desc>`, `fix/issue-<N>-<short-desc>`, `chore/<short-desc>`, `docs/<short-desc>`.
8. **Branch protection on `main`:** require PR, require passing CI, require ≥1 review, no force-push, no direct commits, dismiss stale reviews on new push.
9. **Squash-merge only into `main`** — keeps history linear and matches rule #1.
10. **Conventional commits** (`feat:`, `fix:`, `chore:`, `docs:`, `test:`, `refactor:`) — enables auto-changelog later.
11. **PR template** with checklist: tested manually? linked issue? security implications? schema migration? Configured in `.github/pull_request_template.md`.
12. **`CODEOWNERS`** file auto-routes reviews per area (backend / frontend / infra / MCP).

### C. CI/CD quality gates
13. **Required CI checks before merge:** Ruff (lint), Black `--check` (format), mypy or pyright (types), pytest (from Week 8), frontend lint/format/test.
14. **Secret scanning:** `gitleaks` or `detect-secrets` in pre-commit AND in CI.
15. **SAST:** Bandit (Python) + CodeQL (GitHub Actions) on every PR.
16. **Dependency vulnerability scanning:** Dependabot alerts + auto-PRs for security updates. Pin deps in `environment.yml`, lock with `conda-lock`.

### D. Coding structure & tooling
17. **Lock the coding structure in Week 1.** Layout, module boundaries, naming, error-shape contract, logging patterns. Document in `CONTRIBUTING.md`. Don't drift.
18. **Python tooling:** conda env (`conda create -n dataq python=3.11`), Black formatter (pre-commit + CI gate), Ruff lint, mypy types.
19. **Frontend tooling:** Prettier + ESLint, also locked in Week 1.
20. **12-factor config:** all env-specific config via env vars (Pydantic Settings on backend, Vite env on frontend). No env-specific code branches.

### E. Observability & error handling
21. **Structured logging from Week 1** — JSON logs with `request_id` correlation ID propagated FastAPI → Celery → GX. Recommend `structlog`.
22. **PII redaction at logger level** — failed-check sample rows can contain sensitive data. Redact centrally, not at every call site.
23. **Exception tracking wired Week 1** — App Insights (it's already in the stack) capturing exceptions from the first commit, not added in Week 7.

### F. Database & migrations
24. **Backward-compatible migrations only.** No `DROP COLUMN` + code change in the same PR. Two-step deploys from Week 5 onward.
25. **Migration PR checklist:** rollback plan + "tested up + down locally" tick. Enforced via PR template.

### G. Documentation & decision history
26. **ADRs (Architecture Decision Records)** in `docs/adr/`. One short markdown per significant decision: `0001-gx-only-for-v1.md`, `0002-orchestration-abstraction-adf-airflow.md`, `0003-severity-tier-weights.md`, `0004-trunk-based-branching.md`, etc.
27. **Architecture diagram in repo:** move `context/DataQ_system_architecture.svg` to `docs/architecture.svg` so it lives next to the code.
28. **Local setup script** `scripts/setup.sh` — one command from fresh clone to working dev env (conda env + pre-commit install + docker-compose up + alembic upgrade head + seed data).

### H. Security review cadence
29. **End-of-week quick scan** from Week 2 onward: review dependency vuln alerts, secret scan results, OWASP top-10 spot check on new endpoints, Key Vault access audit.
30. **Hard security review gate before Week 7 deployment** — full pass on all the above plus public-endpoint exposure review (especially `/api/v1/orchestration/events/*` and `/mcp`).

---

## Execution principles

1. **Pierce the stack end-to-end in Week 1**, even if narrow. Auth → API → GX → DB → UI must touch all layers before any horizontal feature work begins. This surfaces integration risk early.
2. **Snowflake is the reference datasource.** Every feature (suites, profiler, execution, results) ships Snowflake-first; flat-file and Unity Catalog are added as parallel adapters once the Snowflake path is validated. **Orchestration integrations (ADF, Airflow) are not datasources** — they are handled by a separate `OrchestrationProvider` abstraction with its own data model (`pipeline_runs`, `trigger_bindings`) distinct from `suites` / `checks`. ADF is the reference orchestration provider; Airflow is the second implementation of the same interface.
3. **Backend before UI, per feature slice.** API + dry-run + tests precede the matching UI. UI work in Week 4/6 assumes a stable API contract from Weeks 2/3/5.
4. **Design decisions that affect DB schema land before code.** Severity tiers (Week 3) and the ADF hybrid model (Week 2) both have schema implications — agree weights, status enum, and webhook contract on day one of their week.
5. **Defer the entire MCP layer to Week 7.** It depends on a stable service layer; building it earlier means rewriting tool docstrings as APIs shift.
6. **Tests are written in the slice they belong to**, not deferred wholesale to Week 8. Week 8 is the *coverage gate and gap-fill* week, not "all testing happens here."

---

## Critical path & dependency graph

```
Week 1: Auth + GX + FastAPI skeleton + DB model
   │
   ├──► Week 2: Datasource CRUD (4 in parallel) + Orchestration (ADF + Airflow)
   │       │
   │       ├──► OrchestrationProvider abstraction ──────────┐
   │       │   ├─ ADF: webhook + trigger bindings           │
   │       │   └─ Airflow: callback webhook + bindings      │
   │       │                                                │
   │       └──► Snowflake / ADLS / S3 / UC connection test  │
   │                │                                       │
   │                ▼                                       │
   │       Week 3: Suite + Check API + Profiler             │
   │                │     (severity tier schema locked)     │
   │                ▼                                       │
   │       Week 4: Connection UI + Check editor UI          │
   │                │                                       │
   │                ▼                                       │
   │       Week 5: Celery execution + Scheduling ◄──────────┤
   │                │              (ADF polling joins here) │
   │                ▼                                       │

   │                                                        │

Week 7: Deployment + Azure Monitor alert setup ◄────────────┘
         + MCP server (8 tools)
   │
   ▼
Week 8: Unit test coverage gate (80%)
```

**Hardest dependency:** Azure Monitor alert rule setup (Week 7) requires the deployed public API URL, which requires Container Apps deployment, which requires CI/CD, which requires a green test suite. If Week 8 slips, ADF webhook end-to-end smoke test slips with it.

---

## Week-by-week execution plan

### Week 1 — Foundation (must end with a vertical slice)

**Exit gate:** A logged-in user (Azure AD) can hit a FastAPI endpoint that triggers GX against a Snowflake DEV table and persists a run result row in Postgres. Swagger live at `/docs`.

**Order of operations within the week:**
1. Day 1: **Lock the coding structure** — repo layout, Python module structure, naming conventions, error-shape contract, logging patterns, commit message format. Conda environment file (`environment.yml`) + Black + Ruff configured. Pre-commit hook running Black. Frontend Prettier + ESLint configured. Commit this as the first PR; everything else builds on it. Document in `CONTRIBUTING.md`.
2. Day 1–2: Monorepo scaffold + Docker Compose (Postgres, Redis, FastAPI, React, Celery worker all reachable from a single `docker-compose up`). Alembic baseline migration with the core data model (`connections`, `suites`, `checks`, `runs`, `results`, `shares`, `pipeline_runs`, `trigger_bindings`). **Schema review checkpoint before merging** — see "Design decisions to lock" below.
3. Day 2–3: Azure AD SSO end-to-end (MSAL token validation in FastAPI; login flow in React). Key Vault wired for credential reads (use a dev Key Vault or local emulator for compose).
4. Day 4–5: GX Core wired to Snowflake DEV. One end-to-end probe endpoint: `POST /api/v1/_probe/snowflake-suite` → runs a hardcoded one-check suite → writes a row to `results`. This is throwaway code; its only job is to prove the wiring.

**Workflow expectations for the week (and every week after):** each numbered item above is a separate PR, manually tested before the next one starts. If any item surfaces a defect (e.g., MSAL token validation fails on edge case), raise a GitHub issue immediately; do not patch silently inside the next PR.

**Risks:**
- MSAL + FastAPI integration is finicky; budget a half-day for token audience/issuer mismatches.
- GX Core v1's Snowflake datasource API changed across point releases — pin GX version on day one.

---

### Week 2 — Datasource connections + Orchestration integrations (ADF + Airflow)

**Exit gate:** All 4 datasource connection types are CRUD-able and testable via API. Both orchestration providers (ADF and Airflow) accept synthetic event payloads through a unified `/api/v1/orchestration/events/{provider}` route and persist to `pipeline_runs`. Trigger-binding schema is in place even if the trigger execution path lands in Week 5.

**Two distinct workstreams this week — do not conflate them in the data model:**

**Workstream A — Datasource connections (4 types):** Snowflake, ADLS Gen2, S3, Unity Catalog. These live in the `connections` table and feed `suites` → `checks` → `runs`. Independent of each other — split across engineers.

**Workstream B — Orchestration integrations (ADF + Airflow):** Orchestrators are *not* datasources. Both providers implement the same `OrchestrationProvider` interface and do three things and nothing else:
1. **Monitor** pipeline/DAG runs (status, duration, failure reason) — stored in `pipeline_runs`, not `results`. The table has a `provider` column (`adf` | `airflow`) and a `provider_run_id`.
2. **Detect failure** in near-real-time via provider-specific event channels (see below).
3. **Trigger suite execution** on successful pipeline/DAG completion — success event maps to a configured suite via `trigger_bindings` (`provider`, `pipeline_or_dag_id`, `suite_id`, `env`) and enqueues a Celery run. This is the only automated trigger mechanism for v1 (REST API trigger is deferred to v1.1).

Neither provider appears in the suite/check editor as a "datasource you can write checks against." Both appear only in: (a) the orchestration status panel on the dashboard, and (b) the trigger-binding UI.

**Provider-specific event channels:**

| Provider | Failure / success channel | Polling fallback |
|---|---|---|
| ADF | Azure Monitor alert rule → webhook `POST /api/v1/orchestration/events/adf` (shared-secret header) | ADF REST API every 10 min (Week 5) |
| Airflow | `on_success_callback` / `on_failure_callback` in DAG → webhook `POST /api/v1/orchestration/events/airflow` (HMAC-signed payload, signing key in Key Vault). Alternative for users who can't add callbacks: Airflow REST API `dagRuns` poller. | Airflow REST API every 10 min (Week 5) |

**Airflow-specific decisions:**
- **Connection record:** Airflow webserver base URL + auth (Basic / token / Kerberos — pick one for v1, default to token). Stored in `connections` with `type=airflow_orchestrator`.
- **Callback adoption is voluntary on the user's side** — we cannot mutate their DAGs. The trigger-binding UI must clearly indicate "this trigger requires the DAG to POST to DataQ on success; copy this callback snippet." Provide a `dataq_airflow_callback` helper snippet (small Python function) in the docs.
- **Polling is the default fallback** for teams who can't add callbacks; documented as higher-latency (up to 10 min delay) vs callback-based near-real-time.

**Critical path:** Unified orchestration event endpoint + provider abstraction + trigger binding schema must land this week — the trigger execution path and polling in Week 5 depend on it. Build the abstraction now; do not hardcode ADF logic and refactor later.

**Design decisions to lock early in the week:**
- `OrchestrationProvider` interface: `parse_event(payload) -> RunUpdate`, `fetch_run_detail(provider_run_id) -> RunDetail`, `list_recent_runs(since) -> [RunUpdate]`. Both ADF and Airflow implementations must conform.
- Authentication strategy per provider: shared secret (ADF, matches Azure Monitor's only auth mode) vs HMAC signature (Airflow, since DAG callbacks can compute signatures). Both secrets in Key Vault.
- `trigger_bindings` schema: composite key (`provider`, `pipeline_or_dag_id`, `env`) → `suite_id`; one pipeline/DAG can map to multiple suites; debounce/dedup behaviour when an event fires twice in quick succession (default: ignore the second trigger if the prior run is still queued/in-progress).
- Failure-event behaviour: failure alerts the user but does **not** trigger a suite run (no point running checks on data that wasn't loaded). Only successful completions trigger runs. Applies to both providers identically.

---

### Week 3 — Suite, check, and profiler API

**Exit gate:** Suites with checks can be created, dry-run, and exported/imported via API across Snowflake, flat files, and UC. Profiler endpoint returns stats for all three.

**Critical design decision — must land Day 1:**
- **Severity tier health-score weights.** Roadmap calls this out explicitly. Agree (e.g., warn=0.5, fail=1.0, critical=2.0) with stakeholders *before* the Alembic migration adds `warn_threshold` / `fail_threshold` / `critical_threshold` columns and the `status` enum. Changing the weight model after results data is written is expensive.

**Sequencing:**
1. Day 1: Severity tier schema migration + status enum decision committed.
2. Day 2–3: Suite/check CRUD + sharing + export/import + dry-run (Snowflake first).
3. Day 4: Profiler service — Snowflake, then ADLS/S3 (Pandas), then UC (Databricks SQL Warehouse). Share a single profiler interface across adapters.
4. Day 5: Flat file batching regex resolution + UC `spark.read.table()` path + cross-source integration tests.

**Framework note (UC path):** Use GX for v1, but keep the UC adapter thin — wrap the GX call behind an `UnityCatalogCheckRunner` interface so the v1.1 DQX adapter (for DLT / streaming) can be swapped in without touching the suite/check/result layer.

---

### Week 4 — Frontend feature parity with API

**Exit gate:** A user can configure any connection type and author a check end-to-end in the browser. No CLI fallback needed.

**Sequencing:**
- Connection manager UI first (it's a precondition for testing the check editor against real data).
- Check editor UI is the heaviest component — budget 3 days. Monaco editor + column profiler panel + dry-run preview + version history drawer is a lot of surface area.
- Suite sharing + admin pages are the lightest — drop to end of week.

**Recommended technical move:** Auto-generate the TypeScript API client from FastAPI's OpenAPI spec (`openapi-typescript-codegen` or similar). Manual fetch hooks across 30+ endpoints will rot fast. **This is the moment to consider promoting the repo to `apps/` + `packages/openapi-client`** if the generated client gets non-trivial.

---

### Week 5 — Execution engine (Celery) + orchestration hybrid monitoring (ADF + Airflow)

**Exit gate:** Suites run async with live per-check progress in the UI. Cron schedules fire. ADF polling fills gaps left by webhooks.

**Sequencing:**
1. Day 1–2: Celery + Redis wired. Run dispatch, progress polling endpoint, cancel.
2. Day 3: Flat file + UC execution paths (Snowflake already works from Week 1 probe).
3. Day 4: Orchestration Celery-beat pollers — one per provider, both implementing the `OrchestrationProvider.list_recent_runs` method from Week 2. ADF poller: 10 min interval against ADF REST API. Airflow poller: 10 min interval against Airflow REST API `/api/v1/dags/~/dagRuns`. Both with 30 min gap-recovery sweep. Critical: polling logic must dedupe against event-updated rows using a `last_updated_at` comparison, not re-fetch unconditionally. **Wire the success-trigger path** (provider-agnostic): on any pipeline/DAG run transitioning to `Succeeded`, look up `trigger_bindings` by (`provider`, `pipeline_or_dag_id`, `env`) and enqueue bound suite runs. Tag the resulting `runs` row with `triggered_by: '<provider>:<pipeline_or_dag_id>:<provider_run_id>'`.
4. Day 5: Scheduling UI + run history UI + retention purge policy.

**Risk:** Celery + FastAPI signal handling on graceful shutdown in Container Apps is fragile. Test cancel under load before Week 6.

---

### Week 6 — Results dashboard + alerting

**Exit gate:** A user with no API access can see health scores, drill into failures, and receive Teams alerts when checks fail.

**Sequencing:**
- Dashboard charts + filter bar first (read-only, low risk).
- Failed-check drill-down (sample failing rows from GX result) is the highest-value feature — prioritise it.
- Alerting last, because dedup + suppression + snooze are stateful and need the results pipeline working to test against.

**Design note:** Severity-aware alert routing (warn = quiet, fail = standard, critical = @channel) is only viable if the Week 3 severity tier model is fully wired. Don't ship alerting if severity is half-done.

---

### Week 7 — Deploy, MCP, harden

**Exit gate:** Production deployment live on Azure Container Apps. MCP server reachable from Claude Desktop with all 8 tools working. Azure Monitor smoke test passes (deliberate ADF failure → webhook fires → DB updates → UI reflects within 5 min).

**Sequencing — strict order:**
1. Day 1–2: Containerise, push to ACR, deploy to Container Apps + Static Web App. CI/CD on `main`. App Insights wired.
2. Day 3: Azure Monitor Action Groups + Alert Rules for nonprod and prod ADF factories (`lll-adf-nonprod`, `lll-adf-prod`). Smoke test end-to-end. **Cannot start until step 1 is live** — needs the public API URL.
3. Day 4: FastMCP scaffold + mount at `/mcp` + Azure AD auth wired to MCP. Implement 4 read-only resources (`list_suites`, `get_suite_results`, `get_health_score`, `get_adf_pipeline_status`).
4. Day 5: Implement 4 write/exec tools (`trigger_suite_run`, `get_run_status`, `create_check`, `profile_column`). LLM-optimised docstrings. Test against Claude Desktop with the 4 canonical natural-language queries from the roadmap.

**Risk concentration:** This is the highest-risk week. Deployment + Azure infra setup + brand-new MCP integration all converge. Budget at least one day of slack; consider pulling MCP work forward into Week 6 evenings if Week 6 alerting wraps early.

---

### Week 8 — Test coverage gate

**Exit gate:** PRs blocked below 80% coverage. Backend (pytest), API (httpx), frontend (Vitest+RTL) all green in CI.

This week is "fill the gaps," not "write all tests now." Tests written incrementally during Weeks 1–7 should already cover the happy paths; Week 8 closes coverage on edge cases (auth rejection, malformed payloads, dedup logic, severity tier evaluation, MCP tool auth, etc.).

**If incremental testing was skipped in earlier weeks, Week 8 will not be enough.** Track coverage weekly from Week 2 onward — don't discover the gap on Week 8 Monday.

---

## Design decisions to lock before coding (cross-week)

| Decision | Week | Why it's load-bearing |
|---|---|---|
| Core DB schema (connections, suites, checks, runs, results, shares) | 1 | Migrations are cheap before data exists, expensive after Week 5. |
| Severity tier weights + `status` enum values | 3 (Day 1) | Schema change + health-score-calc affect every downstream result. |
| ADF webhook shared-secret model + rotation | 2 | Cannot be changed silently after Azure Monitor is configured in Week 7. |
| Health score weighting formula | 3 (Day 1) | Bound to severity tier decision; affects 7-day trend math. |
| Repo layout (flat vs apps/) | 1 | Default flat; revisit only if shared TS package appears. |
| OpenAPI client codegen vs hand-written fetch hooks | 4 | Decide before writing the 2nd manual hook. |
| DQ framework: **GX-only for v1** (DQX deferred to v1.1) | 1 | Unifies result schema, suite model, MCP tools, and check editor across all 4 datasource types. DQX would force a second execution path and result shape for the UC adapter. |
| Coding structure: repo layout, module boundaries, naming, error contracts, logging | 1 (Day 1) | Working-agreement #6 — decide once, follow throughout. Document in `CONTRIBUTING.md`. |
| Python tooling: conda env + Black + Ruff | 1 (Day 1) | Working-agreement #7. CI must reject unformatted Python. |

---

## v1.1 — DQX for Databricks (streaming + DLT)

The roadmap defers "Databricks Live Tables (DLT) expectations" to v1.1. That work is best served by **Databricks Labs DQX**, not GX:

- **Why DQX, not GX, for DLT/streaming:** GX is batch-only; DQX is native to Databricks runtime, supports streaming, and integrates with DLT's Expectations API directly. Running GX-on-Spark for streaming is awkward and high-overhead.
- **Scope of the v1.1 add:** new `DqxCheckRunner` implementing the same `UnityCatalogCheckRunner` interface introduced in Week 3; a result-shape adapter that normalises DQX output into DataQ's existing `check_results` schema (severity tier, status enum, observed/expected); UI toggle on UC suites for `engine: gx | dqx`.
- **What stays GX in v1.1:** batch UC tables via SQL Warehouse (Week 5 path) — no reason to migrate working code. DQX is added alongside, not as a replacement.
- **Prerequisite from v1:** the Week 3 thin-adapter pattern for UC. If that's skipped, v1.1 DQX work doubles in size.

## Cross-cutting risks

1. **Azure AD MSAL gotchas** (Week 1): token audience / issuer / tenant validation. Mitigate: pair with whoever owns the Azure tenant on Day 1.
2. **GX Core v1 API drift** — pin version, don't track latest.
3. **ADF webhook reachability** (Week 7): Container Apps ingress must be public on `/api/v1/adf/events`. Coordinate with infra/security earlier than Week 7 to avoid a deployment-day surprise.
4. **Celery shutdown semantics** (Week 5): Container Apps + graceful cancel needs explicit testing.
5. **MCP descriptor quality** (Week 7): "Implemented" ≠ "tool selection works." Treat the 4 canonical NL queries from the roadmap as acceptance tests, not nice-to-haves.
6. **Coverage debt** (Week 8): track weekly from Week 2, not at the end.

---

## Milestone gates (go/no-go before next week starts)

- **End W1:** Vertical slice runs end-to-end locally. Swagger live. Migration applied cleanly.
- **End W2:** All 4 datasource connection types CRUD-able. Both orchestration providers (ADF + Airflow) accept synthetic event payloads through the unified endpoint and persist trigger bindings via the shared `OrchestrationProvider` abstraction.
- **End W3:** Severity tier model deployed to dev. Dry-run works across all 3 source types.
- **End W4:** UI feature-complete for connection + suite + check authoring. No API-only workflows remain.
- **End W5:** Scheduled run completes overnight in dev across all source types. ADF polling fills gaps.
- **End W6:** Teams alert fires on a deliberate check failure with correct severity routing.
- **End W7:** Production deploy live. Azure Monitor smoke test green. Claude Desktop drives a suite run via MCP.
- **End W8:** Coverage gate ≥80%, CI enforcing.

---

## Verification

This plan is a planning document — verification means stakeholder review, not code execution. Suggested review steps:
1. Walk the dependency graph with the engineer who will own ADF integration — confirm Week 2 → 5 → 7 sequencing is realistic given the team's Azure Monitor access.
2. Confirm severity tier weights with the data product owner *before* Week 3 starts.
3. Confirm Key Vault and Azure tenant access exist *before* Week 1 starts.
4. Each week's exit gate should be demoed on the Friday of that week. If a gate fails, do not start the next week's parallel work — fix the gate first.

### CLAUDE.md outline (to be written in PR 0)

Single source of truth for any AI assistant entering the repo. Sections:

1. **Project summary** — DataQ in one paragraph: GX-based DQ across 4 datasources + 2 orchestration providers, single-tenant, 8-week v1.
2. **Architecture at a glance** — link to `docs/architecture.svg`; brief callouts for FastAPI + Celery + GX + Postgres + Redis + Key Vault + Static Web App + MCP at `/mcp`.
3. **Repo layout** — flat monorepo (`backend/` + `frontend/` + `docs/` + `scripts/`); what lives where; when to promote to `apps/` + `packages/`.
4. **Datasources vs orchestration** — explicit: 4 datasources (Snowflake, ADLS, S3, UC) you can write checks against; 2 orchestration providers (ADF, Airflow) that monitor/trigger only. **Never** treat orchestration as a datasource.
5. **Framework choice** — GX-only for v1; DQX deferred to v1.1 for DLT/streaming. Keep UC adapter thin behind `UnityCatalogCheckRunner` interface.
6. **Working agreements** — link to the 30-rule list in `CONTRIBUTING.md`. Highlights: one-functionality-per-commit, manual test before next feature, defects → GitHub issue (never silent fix), conda + Black + Ruff + mypy, trunk-based branching, squash-merge only, conventional commits.

10. **Critical pointers** — `pipeline_runs` ≠ `runs`; `trigger_bindings` is provider-agnostic; PII redaction at logger level; backward-compatible migrations only; secret scanning in pre-commit; Azure Monitor needs the deployed URL (Week 7 dependency).
11. **What NOT to do** — don't add ADF as a queryable datasource; don't bypass the `OrchestrationProvider` abstraction; don't `--no-verify` past hooks; don't commit `.env`; don't drop columns in same PR as code change; don't fix bugs silently.

Architecture at a glance\n\nSee [docs/architecture.svg](docs/architecture.svg) for the full diagram (moved here from `context/` in PR 0).\n\n```\nBrowser ──HTTPS──► React (Static Web App) ──► FastAPI (Container Apps) ──► PostgreSQL\n                                                    │  │\nAI clients ──MCP/HTTP──► FastAPI /mcp endpoint      │  └──► Celery worker ──► GX execution ──► Snowflake / ADLS / S3 / UC\n                                                    │\n                                                    ├──► Redis (task queue)\n                                                    ├──► Key Vault (secrets)\n                                                    └──► App Insights (observability)\n\nADF ──► Azure Monitor alert rule ──► webhook ──► POST /api/v1/orchestration/events/adf\nAirflow ──► on_success/on_failure_callback ──► POST /api/v1/orchestration/events/airflow\nFastAPI ──► MS Teams webhook (alerts)\n```\n\n---\n\n## 3. Repo layout\n\nFlat monorepo (decided in Week 1):\n\n```\nDataQ/\n├── backend/                     # FastAPI + Celery + GX (Python, conda)\n│   ├── app/\n│   │   ├── core/                # logging, errors, config (locked in PR 2)\n│   │   ├── db/                  # SQLAlchemy models, session\n│   │   ├── api/                 # FastAPI routers (versioned: /api/v1/...)\n│   │   ├── services/            # business logic per domain\n│   │   ├── orchestration/       # OrchestrationProvider abstraction (ADF, Airflow)\n│   │   ├── datasources/         # GX adapter per datasource type\n│   │   └── mcp/                 # FastMCP tools (Week 7)\n│   ├── alembic/\n│   └── tests/\n├── frontend/                    # React + Vite + Ant Design (Node, pnpm or npm)\n│   ├── src/\n│   └── tests/\n├── docs/\n│   ├── architecture.svg\n│   └── adr/                     # Architecture Decision Records\n├── scripts/\n│   └── setup.sh                 # one-command dev env bootstrap\n├── context/                     # original product/roadmap context (read-only reference)\n│   └── DataQ_platform_roadmap.md\n├── .github/\n│   ├── workflows/\n│   ├── pull_request_template.md\n│   └── ISSUE_TEMPLATE/\n├── docker-compose.yml\n├── environment.yml              # conda env definition\n├── conda-lock.yml\n├── pyproject.toml               # Black + Ruff + mypy config\n├── CONTRIBUTING.md\n├── CLAUDE.md                    # this file\n└── README.md\n```\n\n**Promotion to `apps/` + `packages/`:** only if a real shared package emerges (e.g., auto-generated OpenAPI client in Week 4–5). Default flat.\n\n---\n\n## 4. Datasources vs orchestration — critical distinction\n\n**Datasources** are stores you write DQ checks against:\n- Snowflake (DEV/QA/UAT)\n- ADLS Gen2 (flat files)\n- AWS S3 (flat files)\n- Unity Catalog / Databricks\n\n**Orchestration providers** are NOT datasources. They are workflow engines whose pipelines/DAGs we observe and react to. Their *only* three responsibilities in DataQ:\n\n1. **Monitor** pipeline/DAG runs → stored in `pipeline_runs` table (separate from `runs` / `results`).\n2. **Detect failure** in near-real-time via provider-specific event channels (webhook for both).\n3. **Trigger suite execution on successful completion** via `trigger_bindings` (`provider`, `pipeline_or_dag_id`, `suite_id`, `env`). Failure events alert the user but do NOT trigger suite runs.\n\nBoth providers implement a single `OrchestrationProvider` interface — ADF is the reference implementation, Airflow is the second. **Never hardcode ADF-only logic; always go through the abstraction.**\n\n| Provider | Event channel | Auth | Polling fallback |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| ADF | Azure Monitor alert → webhook | Shared secret header (Azure Monitor's only mode) | ADF REST API, 10 min |\n| Airflow | DAG `on_*_callback` → webhook | HMAC-signed payload (signing key in Key Vault) | Airflow REST API `dagRuns`, 10 min |\n\nAirflow callbacks require the user to add a snippet to their DAGs (we can't mutate them). Polling is the documented fallback.\n\n**Anti-pattern (do not do this):** treating ADF/Airflow as a 5th/6th datasource in the connection editor, check editor, or suite model.\n\n---\n\n## 5. Framework choice — GX-only for v1\n\n- **v1:** Great Expectations (GX Core) is the sole DQ framework across all 4 datasources. Unifies result schema, suite/check model, MCP tools, and the check editor.\n- **v1.1:** Databricks Labs **DQX** will be added for DLT / streaming use cases (GX is batch-only and runs poorly on streaming). DQX will implement the same `UnityCatalogCheckRunner` interface introduced in Week 3 — UI exposes `engine: gx | dqx` toggle on UC suites.\n- **Implication for Week 3:** keep the UC adapter thin behind `UnityCatalogCheckRunner` so v1.1 DQX swap-in doesn't ripple into the suite/check/result layer.\n\n---\n\n## 6. Working agreements (rules above feature work)\n\nFull list (30 rules across 8 categories) lives in [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md). Highlights:\n\n### Commit & change discipline\n- **One functionality per commit** (where possible).\n- **Manually test each committed change before starting the next functionality** (required until unit tests land in Week 8).\n- **Defects → GitHub issue, never silent fixes.** Use `gh issue create`. The fixing PR must include `Fixes #N`.\n- **From Week 8 onward, every new functionality ships with tests.**\n\n### Git workflow\n- **Trunk-based** with short-lived feature branches off `main`. No long-lived `develop`.\n- Branch names: `feature/<desc>`, `fix/issue-<N>-<desc>`, `chore/<desc>`, `docs/<desc>`.\n- `main` is protected: PR + ≥1 review + passing CI + no force-push.\n- **Squash-merge only into `main`.**\n- **Conventional commits** (`feat:`, `fix:`, `chore:`, `docs:`, `test:`, `refactor:`).\n\n### CI/CD quality gates (block merge)\n- Ruff (lint), Black `--check` (format), mypy (types), pytest (from W8), frontend lint/format/test.\n- `gitleaks` secret scanning (pre-commit + CI).\n- Bandit (Python SAST) + CodeQL.\n- Dependabot for npm + pip + github-actions.\n\n### Tooling (locked in Week 1, do not drift)\n- **Python:** conda env (`conda create -n dataq python=3.11`) — *not* venv, *not* poetry.\n- **Black** formatter (CI-enforced).\n- **Ruff** lint, **mypy** types, **structlog** logging, **Pydantic Settings** config (12-factor).\n- **Frontend:** Prettier + ESLint.\n\n### Observability\n- **Structured logging from Week 1.** structlog, JSON, `request_id` correlation propagated FastAPI → Celery → GX.\n- **PII redaction at logger level** (failed-check sample rows may contain sensitive data).\n- **App Insights exception tracking wired Week 1**, not Week 7.\n\n### Database\n- **Backward-compatible migrations only.** No `DROP COLUMN` + code change in same PR. Two-step deploys from W5 onward.\n- Migration PR checklist: rollback plan + \"tested up + down locally.\"\n\n### Documentation\n- **ADRs in `docs/adr/`** — one short markdown per significant decision.\n- `scripts/setup.sh` — one command from clone to working dev env.\n\n### Security cadence\n- End-of-week quick scan from Week 2: vuln alerts, secret scan, OWASP spot check, Key Vault audit.\n- Hard security review gate before Week 7 deploy.\n\n---\n\n## 7. Required reading before coding\n\n1. [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) — full 30-rule working agreements + DoD + commit/branch conventions\n2. [docs/adr/](docs/adr/) — all ADRs (architecture decisions with rationale)\n3. [context/DataQ_platform_roadmap.md](context/DataQ_platform_roadmap.md) — the 8-week, 100-task product roadmap\n4. The current week's milestone target (see §13 below)\n\n---\n\n## 8. Local dev quickstart\n\n```bash\ngit clone <repo>\ncd DataQ\n./scripts/setup.sh           # creates conda env, installs pre-commit, pulls images, runs migrations, seeds dev data\nconda activate dataq\ndocker-compose up            # Postgres + Redis + FastAPI + React + Celery worker\n# Smoke test:\ncurl -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/v1/_probe/snowflake-suite\n# Browse Swagger: http://localhost:8000/docs\n```\n\n---\n\n## 9. Key design decisions (with ADR links)\n\n| Decision | ADR | Status |\n|---|---|---|\n| Trunk-based branching, squash-merge into `main` | [0001](docs/adr/0001-trunk-based-branching.md) | Locked W1 |\n| Conventional commits | [0002](docs/adr/0002-conventional-commits.md) | Locked W1 |\n| GX-only for v1; DQX deferred to v1.1 | [0003](docs/adr/0003-gx-only-for-v1.md) | Locked W1 |\n| Orchestration abstraction (ADF + Airflow share `OrchestrationProvider`) | [0004](docs/adr/0004-orchestration-abstraction.md) | Locked W1 |\n| Severity tier weights (warn/fail/critical → health score) | `0005` (TBD W3) | Pending stakeholder agreement before W3 starts |\n| ADF webhook auth (shared secret) + Key Vault rotation | `0006` (TBD W2) | Pending W2 |\n| Airflow callback model (HMAC-signed) + polling fallback | `0007` (TBD W2) | Pending W2 |\n| MCP mounted at `/mcp` with Azure AD auth | `0008` (TBD W7) | Pending W7 |\n| Repo layout: flat monorepo (`backend/` + `frontend/`) | `0009` (TBD W1) | Locked W1 |\n\n---\n\n## 10. Critical pointers (easy to get wrong)\n\n- **`pipeline_runs` ≠ `runs`.** Orchestrator pipeline executions live in `pipeline_runs`; DQ suite executions live in `runs`. They link via `triggered_by: '<provider>:<pipeline_or_dag_id>:<provider_run_id>'`.\n- **`trigger_bindings` is provider-agnostic.** Composite key (`provider`, `pipeline_or_dag_id`, `env`) → `suite_id`. Don't add an ADF-specific bindings table.\n- **PII redaction at the logger level**, not at every call site. The redactor sits in `backend/app/core/logging.py`.\n- **Backward-compatible migrations only.** Code that depends on a new column ships in a separate PR *after* the migration is deployed.\n- **Secret scanning in pre-commit AND CI.** Don't rely on one alone.\n- **Azure Monitor alert setup (Week 7) needs the deployed public API URL.** Deployment must come first; coordinate Container Apps ingress with infra/security before Week 7 to avoid a deployment-day surprise.\n- **MCP tool descriptions are LLM-facing, not REST-API-facing.** Write them for natural-language selection; test against the 4 canonical NL queries in the roadmap.\n\n---\n\n## 11. What NOT to do\n\n- ❌ Don't add ADF or Airflow as a queryable datasource in the connection editor / check editor / suite model.\n- ❌ Don't bypass the `OrchestrationProvider` abstraction with provider-specific branching in service code.\n- ❌ Don't `git commit --no-verify` past hooks. If a hook fails, fix the underlying issue.\n- ❌ Don't commit `.env` files. Use `.env.example` as the template.\n- ❌ Don't drop columns in the same PR as the code change that stops using them. Two-step it.\n- ❌ Don't fix bugs silently. Raise a GitHub issue, then PR with `Fixes #N`.\n- ❌ Don't batch unrelated changes into one commit. One functionality per commit.\n- ❌ Don't track GX Core at \"latest.\" Pin the version in `environment.yml` — GX v1 API has drifted across point releases.\n- ❌ Don't use venv or poetry for backend dev. Conda only.\n- ❌ Don't write the MCP layer before Week 7. The service layer must stabilise first.\n\n---\n\n## 12. Where things live\n\n| Artifact | Location |\n|---|---|\n| Product roadmap (100 tasks, 8 weeks) | [context/DataQ_platform_roadmap.md](context/DataQ_platform_roadmap.md) |\n| System architecture diagram | [docs/architecture.svg](docs/architecture.svg) |\n| Architecture Decision Records | [docs/adr/](docs/adr/) |\n| Working agreements (full 30-rule list) | [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) |\n| Execution plan (sequencing, gates, risks) | Reference plan: `~/.claude/plans/hey-create-the-project-inherited-flute.md` (will be committed to `docs/execution-plan.md` in PR 0) |\n| Memory (cross-session AI context) | `~/.claude/projects/-Users-arijit-Coding-Python-DataQ/memory/` |\n\n---\n\n## 13. > AGENT

Quick note before I add the rule — on a public repo, "only collaborators can change the repo" mostly happens by default:

- ✅ **Push to any branch** — already collaborators-only (GitHub baseline)
- ✅ **Merge PRs** — already collaborators-only
- ⚠️ **Open a PR from a fork** — anyone can; you decide whether to merge (the review gate handles this — outsider PRs sit in the queue)
- ⚠️ **Open issues / discussions** — anyone with a GitHub account can, unless explicitly disabled
- ❌ **Fork the repo** — anyone can; this *cannot* be disabled on public repos

So push/merge are already locked. The decisions are: (a) belt-and-braces ruleset restricting pushes to you explicitly, and (b) whether to lock down issues/discussions.

{
  "file_path": "/Users/arijit/Coding/Python/DataQ/docs/adr/0001-trunk-based-branching.md",
  "content": "# ADR 0001 — Trunk-based branching with squash-merge into `main`\n\n- **Status:** Accepted\n- **Date:** 2026-05-24\n- **Deciders:** @TheurgicDuke771\n\n## Context\n\nDataQ v1 has an 8-week timeline and a small team (starting solo, expected to grow). We need a branching model that supports frequent integration, keeps `main` history readable, and aligns with the working-agreement of one functionality per commit.\n\n## Decision\n\nAdopt **trunk-based development** with short-lived feature branches off `main`, and **squash-merge** as the only allowed merge method into `main`.\n\n- All work happens on a branch named `feature/<desc>`, `fix/issue-<N>-<desc>`, `chore/<desc>`, or `docs/<desc>`.\n- Branches are short-lived (ideally hours to a couple of days), opened as PRs against `main`.\n- PRs are squash-merged — the PR title becomes the single commit on `main` (so PR titles MUST follow conventional commits — see ADR 0002).\n- No long-lived `develop` branch.\n- `main` is protected via a GitHub ruleset (deletion blocked, force-push blocked, linear history required, PR required, squash-only merge, dismiss stale reviews on new push). Admin (sole maintainer) can bypass in emergencies.\n- Auto-delete head branches on merge.\n\n## Consequences\n\n**Positive**\n- `main` history reads as one commit per delivered functionality — matches working-agreement #1.\n- Short-lived branches force small, reviewable changes.\n- No long-lived branches to keep in sync.\n- Linear history makes `git bisect` reliable.\n\n**Negative**\n- Loses individual WIP commits inside a PR. Mitigated: those commits remain visible in the PR view on GitHub.\n- Solo dev currently has `required_approving_review_count: 0` — must bump to 1 when a second contributor joins (tracked as a future change).\n\n## Alternatives considered\n\n- **GitFlow** — rejected. The `develop` / `release` / `hotfix` overhead is unjustified for an 8-week single-tenant v1; release cadence is continuous, not versioned.\n- **Merge commits preserving branch history** — rejected. Squash gives one commit per functionality on `main`; preserved branch history would dilute that signal and clutter `git log`.\n- **Rebase-and-merge** — rejected. Preserves all WIP commits on `main`, breaking the one-functionality-per-commit principle.\n"
}
```

{
  "file_path": "/Users/arijit/Coding/Python/DataQ/docs/adr/0002-conventional-commits.md",
  "content": "# ADR 0002 — Conventional commits for PR titles and commit messages\n\n- **Status:** Accepted\n- **Date:** 2026-05-24\n- **Deciders:** @TheurgicDuke771\n\n## Context\n\nWith squash-merge as the only allowed merge method (ADR 0001), each PR becomes exactly one commit on `main` whose message is the PR title. The PR title format therefore drives the readability of `git log` and enables future automation (changelog generation, release notes).\n\n## Decision\n\nUse **Conventional Commits** for all PR titles and individual commits.\n\nAllowed type prefixes:\n\n| Type | Use for |\n|---|---|\n| `feat:` | New user-facing functionality |\n| `fix:` | Bug fix (PR body MUST include `Fixes #N` per working-agreement #3) |\n| `chore:` | Tooling, dependencies, repo housekeeping |\n| `docs:` | Documentation-only change (CLAUDE.md, ADRs, README, code comments) |\n| `test:` | Test-only change |\n| `refactor:` | Internal change with no behaviour change |\n\nFormat: `<type>(<optional-scope>): <imperative summary>`\n\nExamples:\n- `feat(orchestration): add Airflow callback webhook handler`\n- `fix(adf): debounce duplicate trigger events within 30s window`\n- `chore: pin GX Core to 1.x`\n- `docs: add ADR 0005 for severity tier weights`\n\n## Consequences\n\n**Positive**\n- `git log --oneline` reads as a categorised changelog.\n- Enables future tooling: auto-changelog, release-please, semantic versioning.\n- PR titles are self-documenting.\n\n**Negative**\n- One more thing for new contributors to learn. Mitigated: the PR template includes a \"Type of change\" checklist that nudges the right prefix.\n\n## Enforcement\n\n- PR template includes the convention.\n- Future enhancement (post-W1): a GitHub Action that fails CI if the PR title does not match the convention.\n"
}
